item.title: As the US Juggles Wars in Iran and Ukraine, North Korea Is a Wildcard
item.description: The US military can generally handle one major crisis, and even a second challenge, but a third would stretch its capacity.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Karl

item.title: We’re Having the Wrong Debate About AI Safety
item.description: China’s embrace of open-source artificial intelligence is giving Silicon Valley a run for its money. It’s also become a major source of clout for Beijing, luring international developers and emerging as a cornerstone of President Xi Jinping’s pitch for collaboration with the Global South and influence over the next tech revolution.
item.dc:creator: Catherine Thorbecke

item.title: Why Zhu Rongji's Death Has Made China Wistful for the 1990s
item.description: The death of a beloved leader has often presented challenges for China’s ruling Communist Party. With few avenues for overtly criticizing the regime, public mourning can become an expression of broader discontent.
item.dc:creator: Juliana Liu

item.title: Under Trump, America's Pivot to Asia Takes a U-Turn
item.description: Lacking a coherent or even discernible strategy in geopolitics, Donald Trump has inadvertently reversed the direction in which American foreign and security policy was going for the past three presidential administrations, including his first. Two more veers took place this week in Asia.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Kluth

item.title: South Korea Makes Billions, and Takes Home Little
item.description: South Korea, home to the world’s two-largest memory chipmakers, is in the midst of an AI-fueled exports boom. Generating wealth and keeping it at home isn’t the same thing, however.
item.dc:creator: Shuli Ren

item.title: Humanoid Robots Need a Supply Chain in North America
item.description: More than a decade ago, hundreds of US garage entrepreneurs were working on shoestring budgets to develop drones with dreams of scaling the new technology. Then China’s DJI introduced a small, inexpensive drone with a stable built-in camera.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Black

item.title: LinkedIn Profile Revisions Are Their Own Form of Job Market Data
item.description: LinkedIn was in large part designed to help people find jobs. It has inadvertently become a treasure trove for economists studying the modern labor market. One research team, for example, used LinkedIn to fill a gap in traditional data, analyzing layoffs and promotions by race, ethnicity and gender — ultimately finding discrimination at some of the companies it studied. item.dc:creator: Beth Kowitt

item.title: Primary Results: Democrats’ Greatest Divide for 2028 Is Education
item.description: Overeducated and underpaid: Welcome to the rising faction of voters pushing the Democratic Party to the socialist left and foreshadowing a clash with mainstream liberals in 2028.
item.dc:creator: David M. Drucker

item.title: California Knows Business-Friendly Rules Stifle Innovation
item.description: California is leading a group of 12 states suing to block Paramount Skydance Corp.’s $110 billion purchase of Warner Bros Discovery Inc., claiming the deal would give the combined company unfair control of movie and cable-TV businesses. Paramount executives responded by threatening to pull its operations out of the Golden State and go to where it’s wanted.
item.dc:creator: Gautam Mukunda

item.title: Acemoglu's New Book Seeks to Restore Liberalism
item.description: Daron Acemoglu’s new book, What Happened to Liberal Democracy?, is deservedly commanding a lot of attention. One of the world’s most eminent economists, the author combines extraordinary historical breadth, cutting-edge technical expertise and a stunning level of academic productivity. He’s co-written excellent popular works on why some countries grew rich and others didn’t, about technology and progress, and about the challenge of creating and sustaining liberty. item.dc:creator: Clive Crook

item.title: The 30-Year Itch Comes for Bonds — and Brazil
item.description: In both cases, investors have cause for concern.
item.dc:creator: John Authers

item.title: Why Iran’s New Leaders Need to Continue the War
item.description: Earlier this year, as the Islamic Republic of Iran was busy crushing the largest protests since those in the aftermath of the 1979 revolution, President Donald Trump promised that help was on its way. He meant, of course, that the US would ride to the rescue of the ordinary Iranians being slaughtered in the streets. Instead, he launched a war that’s given a new lease on life to the regime that was killing them.
item.dc:creator: Marc Champion

item.title: AI's Tendency to Lie and Cheat Is Written Into Its Training
item.description: Artificial intelligence models are trained not to lie to humans. Yet a funny thing is happening: AI has been lying to humans quite a bit.
item.dc:creator: Parmy Olson

item.title: UK's Social Care Morass May Be Andy Burnham’s Biggest Test Yet
item.description: Develop brain cancer in England and the National Health Service largely covers you. Get diagnosed with dementia and you may pay until your savings are depleted — and even then some bills keep coming. A parliamentary committee summed up the system as “unfair, confusing, demeaning and frightening.” Some might call that British understatement.
item.dc:creator: The Editors

item.title: Germany Is Seeking Peace in UniCredit’s Commerzbank Victory
item.description: The German government is finally accepting the inevitable: UniCredit Group SpA has essentially won the battle for Commerzbank AG. The finance ministry still holds a stake in Commerzbank and is seeking a gracious exit after bitterly opposing the Italian takeover. item.dc:creator: Paul J. Davies
